reason: The provided sources offer multiple overlapping accounts from distinct sites to construct a detailed, multi-perspective narrative of Custer's famous defeat, supported by more than 15 well-cited claims.
story: In June 1876, Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer marched his 7th Cavalry into the Montana Territory. Driven by gold discoveries in the sacred Black Hills, the U.S. government sought to force the Lakota and Cheyenne onto reservations. Weeks prior, spiritual leader Sitting Bull had envisioned U.S. soldiers falling like grasshoppers into his camp. Unaware that a supporting column under General Crook had already been forced to retreat at the Rosebud River, Custer ignored his Crow scouts' warnings of an immense, unprecedented village. Instead of waiting, Custer split his forces to prevent the Native Americans from scattering. Major Marcus Reno charged first but was quickly overwhelmed, fleeing in a chaotic, bloody rout to the bluffs. Left entirely isolated, Custer and his five companies were swiftly surrounded. Armed with repeating rifles, the warriors annihilated Custer’s immediate command of approximately 210 men in under an hour, leaving Custer dead with two bullet wounds.
angle: Weeks before Custer marched to his doom, the Lakota spiritual leader Sitting Bull had a terrifyingly accurate vision of U.S. soldiers falling from the sky like grasshoppers into his camp.

claims.claim: The Battle of the Little Bighorn, also known as the Battle of the Greasy Grass, occurred on June 25–26, 1876, in Montana Territory.
The conflict arose after gold was discovered in the sacred Black Hills, prompting prospectors to violate treaties and flood the region.
Sitting Bull, a Lakota spiritual leader, had a vision of U.S. soldiers falling into his camp like grasshoppers weeks before the battle.
General George Crook's supporting army column was forced to withdraw after being defeated at the Battle of the Rosebud on June 17, 1876.
Custer commanded the 7th Cavalry Regiment during the 1876 campaign.
Custer divided his forces into three main battalions under himself, Major Marcus Reno, and Captain Frederick Benteen.
Major Reno was ordered to cross the river and attack the southern end of the Indian encampment.
Reno's assault failed, and his forces retreated in a chaotic rout back across the river to the bluffs.
Custer sent a famous final written message to Benteen, urging him to 'Come on, Big Village, Be quick, Bring packs.'
Neither Reno nor Benteen moved to reinforce Custer's battalion, despite hearing heavy gunfire from his position.
Custer and all of the men in his immediate five-company battalion, numbering approximately 210 men, were completely wiped out.
The battle resulted in 268 total U.S. military fatalities.
Estimated Native American casualties in the battle were around 60 to 100 dead.
Custer's body was recovered with two bullet wounds, one to his temple and one to his chest.
Following the battle, the U.S. Army intensified its efforts, forcing most Plains Indians onto reservations within a year.
Crazy Horse surrendered in May 1877 and was killed later that year.
Sitting Bull escaped to Canada before surrendering in 1881, and was ultimately killed in 1890.

disputed: Whether Custer attempted to cross the river at Minneconjou Ford (Medicine Tail Ford) is highly disputed by different historical witnesses. A script should attribute this, noting that some Native scouts claimed he tried to cross and was driven back, while others, including Chief Gall, stated he never reached the water.

Whether Custer directly disobeyed orders is treated inconsistently across sources. A script should handle this neutrally by explaining that while some sources accuse him of disobeying, his official orders did grant him the flexibility to depart from the plan based on local conditions.
